title: Adaptation to Climate Change: Evidence from US Agriculture
research_question: To what extent have agricultural producers in the United States adapted to longer-run changes in temperature and precipitation, and how do these longer-run adjustments compare to short-run responses to weather fluctuations? What are the implications of any observed adaptation (or lack thereof) for the projected impacts of future climate change on crop productivity?
data_description: The analysis uses county-level data on US agriculture, primarily focused on counties east of the 100th meridian, which account for the bulk of US corn and soy production. Crop yield and area data come from the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service at the county-year level, while revenue, expenditure, and land value measures come from the Agricultural Census conducted every five years. Climate data are drawn from Schlenker and Roberts (2009) and consist of daily interpolated maximum/minimum temperatures and precipitation for 4km grid cells over 1950–2005, aggregated to county-day values over cropped areas. Key variables include growing degree days (with piecewise linear thresholds, e.g., above/below 29°C), growing-season precipitation, corn and soy yields, crop revenues, input expenditures, farm counts, county population, crop insurance take-up, and county-level political and educational covariates. The primary sample period spans 1980–2000, with robustness over 1950–2005.
institutional_context: The setting is US field-crop agriculture during a period of substantial and spatially heterogeneous climate change. Between 1980 and 2000, growing-season temperatures rose by up to 1.5°C in some counties while falling by 0.5°C in others, and precipitation changed by ±40 percent across counties—variation that largely spans near-term projections from global climate models. Corn and soy dominate US cropping, with corn playing a central role in domestic and global food and fuel markets. The period also saw growing public and scientific awareness of climate change, alongside major federal agricultural support programs, including a large mid-1990s expansion of subsidized crop insurance that tripled program participation. Physical-science evidence attributes the heterogeneous warming pattern largely to natural ocean-driven climate variability, supporting a quasi-experimental interpretation of recent climate trends. The setting allows assessment of whether farmers' production choices, input use, crop mix, farm exit, and insurance uptake responded to multi-decade climatic changes.
